gene.name: ATP binding cassette subfamily A member 4
gene.function: Flippase that catalyzes in an ATP-dependent manner the transport of retinal-phosphatidylethanolamine conjugates like 11-cis and all-trans isomers of N-retinylidene-phosphatidylethanolamine (N- Ret-PE) from the lumen to the cytoplasmic leaflet of photoreceptor outer segment disk membranes, where 11-cis-retinylidene- phosphatidylethanolamine is then isomerized to its all-trans isomer and reduced by RDH8 to produce all-trans-retinol. This transport activity ensures that all-trans-retinal generated from photoexcitation and 11- cis-retinal not needed for the regeneration of rhodopsin and cone opsins are effectively cleared from the photoreceptors, therefore preventing their accumulation and the formation of toxic bisretinoid. Displays ATPase activity in vitro in absence of retinal substrate. May display GTPase activity that is strongly influenced by the lipid environment and the presence of retinoid compounds. Binds the unprotonated form of N-retinylidene-phosphatidylethanolamine with high affinity in the absence of ATP, and ATP binding and hydrolysis induce a protein conformational change that causes N-retinylidene- phosphatidylethanolamine release (By similarity).

gene.name: angiotensin I converting enzyme
gene.function: Dipeptidyl carboxypeptidase that removes dipeptides from the C-terminus of a variety of circulating hormones, such as angiotensin I, bradykinin or enkephalins, thereby playing a key role in the regulation of blood pressure, electrolyte homeostasis or synaptic plasticity. Composed of two similar catalytic domains, each possessing a functional active site, with different selectivity for substrates. Plays a major role in the angiotensin-renin system that regulates blood pressure and sodium retention by the kidney by converting angiotensin I to angiotensin II, resulting in an increase of the vasoconstrictor activity of angiotensin. Also able to inactivate bradykinin, a potent vasodilator, and therefore enhance the blood pressure response. Acts as a regulator of synaptic transmission by mediating cleavage of neuropeptide hormones, such as substance P, neurotensin or enkephalins. Catalyzes degradation of different enkephalin neuropeptides (Met- enkephalin, Leu-enkephalin, Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe and possibly Met- enkephalin-Arg-Gly-Leu). Acts as a regulator of synaptic plasticity in the nucleus accumbens of the brain by mediating cleavage of Met-enkephalin- Arg-Phe, a strong ligand of Mu-type opioid receptor OPRM1, into Met- enkephalin (By similarity). Met-enkephalin-Arg-Phe cleavage by ACE decreases activation of OPRM1, leading to long-term synaptic potentiation of glutamate release (By similarity). Also acts as a regulator of hematopoietic stem cell differentiation by mediating degradation of hemoregulatory peptide N-acetyl-SDKP (AcSDKP). Acts as a regulator of cannabinoid signaling pathway by mediating degradation of hemopressin, an antagonist peptide of the cannabinoid receptor CNR1. Involved in amyloid-beta metabolism by catalyzing degradation of Amyloid-beta protein 40 and Amyloid-beta protein 42 peptides, thereby preventing plaque formation. Catalyzes cleavage of cholecystokinin (maturation of Cholecystokinin-8 and Cholecystokinin-5) and Gonadoliberin-1 (both maturation and degradation) hormones. Degradation of hemoregulatory peptide N-acetyl-SDKP (AcSDKP) and amyloid-beta proteins is mediated by the N-terminal catalytic domain, while angiotensin I and cholecystokinin cleavage is mediated by the C-terminal catalytic region.

gene.name: actinin alpha 3
gene.function: F-actin cross-linking protein which is thought to anchor actin to a variety of intracellular structures. This is a bundling protein.

gene.name: angiotensinogen
gene.function: Essential component of the renin-angiotensin system (RAS), a potent regulator of blood pressure, body fluid and electrolyte homeostasis.

gene.name: BCL2 associated X, apoptosis regulator
gene.function: Plays a role in the mitochondrial apoptotic process. Under normal conditions, BAX is largely cytosolic via constant retrotranslocation from mitochondria to the cytosol mediated by BCL2L1/Bcl-xL, which avoids accumulation of toxic BAX levels at the mitochondrial outer membrane (MOM). Under stress conditions, undergoes a conformation change that causes translocation to the mitochondrion membrane, leading to the release of cytochrome c that then triggers apoptosis. Promotes activation of CASP3, and thereby apoptosis.

gene.name: BCL2 apoptosis regulator
gene.function: Suppresses apoptosis in a variety of cell systems including factor-dependent lymphohematopoietic and neural cells. Regulates cell death by controlling the mitochondrial membrane permeability. Appears to function in a feedback loop system with caspases. Inhibits caspase activity either by preventing the release of cytochrome c from the mitochondria and/or by binding to the apoptosis-activating factor (APAF-1). Also acts as an inhibitor of autophagy: interacts with BECN1 and AMBRA1 during non-starvation conditions and inhibits their autophagy function. May attenuate inflammation by impairing NLRP1- inflammasome activation, hence CASP1 activation and IL1B release.

gene.name: catalase
gene.function: Catalyzes the degradation of hydrogen peroxide (H(2)O(2)) generated by peroxisomal oxidases to water and oxygen, thereby protecting cells from the toxic effects of hydrogen peroxide. Promotes growth of cells including T-cells, B-cells, myeloid leukemia cells, melanoma cells, mastocytoma cells and normal and transformed fibroblast cells. .

gene.name: cell division cycle 37, HSP90 cochaperone
gene.function: Co-chaperone that binds to numerous kinases and promotes their interaction with the Hsp90 complex, resulting in stabilization and promotion of their activity. Inhibits HSP90AA1 ATPase activity.

gene.name: forkhead box O1
gene.function: Transcription factor that is the main target of insulin signaling and regulates metabolic homeostasis in response to oxidative stress. Binds to the insulin response element (IRE) with consensus sequence 5'-TT[G/A]TTTTG-3' and the related Daf-16 family binding element (DBE) with consensus sequence 5'-TT[G/A]TTTAC-3'. Activity suppressed by insulin. Main regulator of redox balance and osteoblast numbers and controls bone mass (By similarity). Orchestrates the endocrine function of the skeleton in regulating glucose metabolism (By similarity). Also acts as a key regulator of chondrogenic commitment of skeletal progenitor cells in response to lipid availability: when lipids levels are low, translocates to the nucleus and promotes expression of SOX9, which induces chondrogenic commitment and suppresses fatty acid oxidation (By similarity). Acts synergistically with ATF4 to suppress osteocalcin/BGLAP activity, increasing glucose levels and triggering glucose intolerance and insulin insensitivity (By similarity). Also suppresses the transcriptional activity of RUNX2, an upstream activator of osteocalcin/BGLAP (By similarity). Acts as an inhibitor of glucose sensing in pancreatic beta cells by acting as a transcription repressor and suppressing expression of PDX1 (By similarity). In hepatocytes, promotes gluconeogenesis by acting together with PPARGC1A and CEBPA to activate the expression of genes such as IGFBP1, G6PC1 and PCK1 (By similarity). Also promotes gluconeogenesis by directly promoting expression of PPARGC1A and G6PC1. Important regulator of cell death acting downstream of CDK1, PKB/AKT1 and STK4/MST1. Promotes neural cell death. Mediates insulin action on adipose tissue (By similarity). Regulates the expression of adipogenic genes such as PPARG during preadipocyte differentiation and, adipocyte size and adipose tissue-specific gene expression in response to excessive calorie intake (By similarity). Regulates the transcriptional activity of GADD45A and repair of nitric oxide-damaged DNA in beta-cells (By similarity). Required for the autophagic cell death induction in response to starvation or oxidative stress in a transcription-independent manner. Mediates the function of MLIP in cardiomyocytes hypertrophy and cardiac remodeling (By similarity). Positive regulator of apoptosis in cardiac smooth muscle cells as a result of its transcriptional activation of pro-apoptotic genes. Regulates endothelial cell (EC) viability and apoptosis in a PPIA/CYPA- dependent manner via transcription of CCL2 and BCL2L11 which are involved in EC chemotaxis and apoptosis.

gene.name: glucose-6-phosphatase catalytic subunit 1
gene.function: Hydrolyzes glucose-6-phosphate to glucose in the endoplasmic reticulum. Forms with the glucose-6-phosphate transporter (SLC37A4/G6PT) the complex responsible for glucose production in the terminal step of glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Hence, it is the key enzyme in homeostatic regulation of blood glucose levels.

gene.name: alpha glucosidase
gene.function: Essential for the degradation of glycogen in lysosomes. Has highest activity on alpha-1,4-linked glycosidic linkages, but can also hydrolyze alpha-1,6-linked glucans.

gene.name: glucosylceramidase beta 1
gene.function: Glucosylceramidase that catalyzes, within the lysosomal compartment, the hydrolysis of glucosylceramides/GlcCers (such as beta- D-glucosyl-(1<->1')-N-acylsphing-4-enine) into free ceramides (such as N-acylsphing-4-enine) and glucose. Plays a central role in the degradation of complex lipids and the turnover of cellular membranes. Through the production of ceramides, participates in the PKC-activated salvage pathway of ceramide formation. Catalyzes the glucosylation of cholesterol, through a transglucosylation reaction where glucose is transferred from GlcCer to cholesterol. GlcCer containing mono-unsaturated fatty acids (such as beta-D- glucosyl-N-(9Z-octadecenoyl)-sphing-4-enine) are preferred as glucose donors for cholesterol glucosylation when compared with GlcCer containing same chain length of saturated fatty acids (such as beta-D- glucosyl-N-octadecanoyl-sphing-4-enine). Under specific conditions, may alternatively catalyze the reverse reaction, transferring glucose from cholesteryl 3-beta-D-glucoside to ceramide (Probable). Can also hydrolyze cholesteryl 3-beta-D- glucoside producing glucose and cholesterol. Catalyzes the hydrolysis of galactosylceramides/GalCers (such as beta-D-galactosyl-(1<->1')-N- acylsphing-4-enine), as well as the transfer of galactose between GalCers and cholesterol in vitro, but with lower activity than with GlcCers. Contrary to GlcCer and GalCer, xylosylceramide/XylCer (such as beta-D-xyosyl-(1<->1')-N-acylsphing-4- enine) is not a good substrate for hydrolysis, however it is a good xylose donor for transxylosylation activity to form cholesteryl 3-beta- D-xyloside. Can also metabolize plant glycosyl phytosterols such as glucosylstigmasterol.

gene.name: galactosidase alpha
gene.function: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of glycosphingolipids and participates in their degradation in the lysosome. .

gene.name: glucagon like peptide 1 receptor
gene.function: G protein-coupled receptor for glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP- 1). Ligand binding triggers activation of a signaling cascade that leads to the activation of adenylyl cyclase and increased intracellular cAMP levels. Plays a role in regulating insulin secretion in response to GLP-1 (By similarity).

gene.name: heat shock protein 90 beta family member 1
gene.function: ATP-dependent chaperone involved in the processing of proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, regulating their transport. Together with MESD, acts as a modulator of the Wnt pathway by promoting the folding of LRP6, a coreceptor of the canonical Wnt pathway. When associated with CNPY3, required for proper folding of Toll-like receptors. Promotes folding and trafficking of TLR4 to the cell surface. May participate in the unfolding of cytosolic leaderless cargos (lacking the secretion signal sequence) such as the interleukin 1/IL-1 to facilitate their translocation into the ERGIC (endoplasmic reticulum- Golgi intermediate compartment) and secretion; the translocation process is mediated by the cargo receptor TMED10.

gene.function: Lysosomal enzyme involved in the degradation pathway of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate.

gene.name: alpha-L-iduronidase
gene.function: Lysosomal hydrolase responsible for the degradation of the glycosaminoglycans heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. .

gene.name: insulin like growth factor 2
gene.function: The insulin-like growth factors possess growth-promoting activity (By similarity). Major fetal growth hormone in mammals. Plays a key role in regulating fetoplacental development. IGF2 is influenced by placental lactogen. Also involved in tissue differentiation. In adults, involved in glucose metabolism in adipose tissue, skeletal muscle and liver (Probable). Acts as a ligand for integrin which is required for IGF2 signaling. Positively regulates myogenic transcription factor MYOD1 function by facilitating the recruitment of transcriptional coactivators, thereby controlling muscle terminal differentiation (By similarity). Inhibits myoblast differentiation and modulates metabolism via increasing the mitochondrial respiration rate (By similarity).

gene.name: insulin like growth factor 2 receptor
gene.function: Mediates the transport of phosphorylated lysosomal enzymes from the Golgi complex and the cell surface to lysosomes. Lysosomal enzymes bearing phosphomannosyl residues bind specifically to mannose-6-phosphate receptors in the Golgi apparatus and the resulting receptor-ligand complex is transported to an acidic prelysosomal compartment where the low pH mediates the dissociation of the complex. The receptor is then recycled back to the Golgi for another round of trafficking through its binding to the retromer. This receptor also binds IGF2. Acts as a positive regulator of T-cell coactivation by binding DPP4.

gene.name: MYD88 innate immune signal transduction adaptor
gene.function: Adapter protein involved in the Toll-like receptor and IL-1 receptor signaling pathway in the innate immune response. Acts via IRAK1, IRAK2, IRF7 and TRAF6, leading to NF-kappa-B activation, cytokine secretion and the inflammatory response. Increases IL-8 transcription. Involved in IL-18- mediated signaling pathway. Activates IRF1 resulting in its rapid migration into the nucleus to mediate an efficient induction of IFN- beta, NOS2/INOS, and IL12A genes. Upon TLR8 activation by GU-rich single-stranded RNA (GU-rich RNA) derived from viruses such as SARS- CoV-2, SARS-CoV and HIV-1, induces IL1B release through NLRP3 inflammasome activation. MyD88-mediated signaling in intestinal epithelial cells is crucial for maintenance of gut homeostasis and controls the expression of the antimicrobial lectin REG3G in the small intestine (By similarity).

gene.name: proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9
gene.function: Crucial player in the regulation of plasma cholesterol homeostasis. Binds to low-density lipid receptor family members: low density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR), very low density lipoprotein receptor (VLDLR), apolipoprotein E receptor (LRP1/APOER) and apolipoprotein receptor 2 (LRP8/APOER2), and promotes their degradation in intracellular acidic compartments. Acts via a non- proteolytic mechanism to enhance the degradation of the hepatic LDLR through a clathrin LDLRAP1/ARH-mediated pathway. May prevent the recycling of LDLR from endosomes to the cell surface or direct it to lysosomes for degradation. Can induce ubiquitination of LDLR leading to its subsequent degradation. Inhibits intracellular degradation of APOB via the autophagosome/lysosome pathway in a LDLR-independent manner. Involved in the disposal of non-acetylated intermediates of BACE1 in the early secretory pathway. Inhibits epithelial Na(+) channel (ENaC)-mediated Na(+) absorption by reducing ENaC surface expression primarily by increasing its proteasomal degradation. Regulates neuronal apoptosis via modulation of LRP8/APOER2 levels and related anti-apoptotic signaling pathways.

gene.name: sirtuin 3
gene.function: NAD-dependent protein deacetylase. Activates or deactivates mitochondrial target proteins by deacetylating key lysine residues. Known targets include ACSS1, IDH, GDH, SOD2, PDHA1, LCAD, SDHA, MRPL12 and the ATP synthase subunit ATP5PO. Contributes to the regulation of the cellular energy metabolism. Important for regulating tissue-specific ATP levels. In response to metabolic stress, deacetylates transcription factor FOXO3 and recruits FOXO3 and mitochondrial RNA polymerase POLRMT to mtDNA to promote mtDNA transcription. Acts as a regulator of ceramide metabolism by mediating deacetylation of ceramide synthases CERS1, CERS2 and CERS6, thereby increasing their activity and promoting mitochondrial ceramide accumulation (By similarity). Regulates hepatic lipogenesis (By similarity). Uses NAD(+) substrate imported by SLC25A47, triggering downstream activation of PRKAA1/AMPK- alpha signaling cascade that ultimately down-regulates sterol regulatory element-binding protein (SREBP) transcriptional activities and ATP-consuming lipogenesis to restore cellular energy balance (By similarity). In addition to protein deacetylase activity, also acts as a protein-lysine deacylase by recognizing other acyl groups, such as benzoyl and lactoyl, leading to protein debenzoylation and delactylation, respectively. Catalyzes debenzoylation of PPIF and ACLY. Mediates delactylation of CCNE2 and 'Lys-16' of histone H4 (H4K16la).

gene.name: survival of motor neuron 1, telomeric
gene.function: The SMN complex catalyzes the assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), the building blocks of the spliceosome, and thereby plays an important role in the splicing of cellular pre- mRNAs. Most spliceosomal snRNPs contain a common set of Sm proteins SNRPB, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG that assemble in a heptameric protein ring on the Sm site of the small nuclear RNA to form the core snRNP (Sm core). In the cytosol, the Sm proteins SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG are trapped in an inactive 6S pICln-Sm complex by the chaperone CLNS1A that controls the assembly of the core snRNP. To assemble core snRNPs, the SMN complex accepts the trapped 5Sm proteins from CLNS1A forming an intermediate. Within the SMN complex, SMN1 acts as a structural backbone and together with GEMIN2 it gathers the Sm complex subunits. Binding of snRNA inside 5Sm ultimately triggers eviction of the SMN complex, thereby allowing binding of SNRPD3 and SNRPB to complete assembly of the core snRNP. Ensures the correct splicing of U12 intron- containing genes that may be important for normal motor and proprioceptive neurons development. Also required for resolving RNA-DNA hybrids created by RNA polymerase II, that form R- loop in transcription terminal regions, an important step in proper transcription termination. May also play a role in the metabolism of small nucleolar ribonucleoprotein (snoRNPs).

gene.function: The SMN complex catalyzes the assembly of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs), the building blocks of the spliceosome, and thereby plays an important role in the splicing of cellular pre- mRNAs. Most spliceosomal snRNPs contain a common set of Sm proteins SNRPB, SNRPD1, SNRPD2, SNRPD3, SNRPE, SNRPF and SNRPG that assemble in a heptameric protein ring on the Sm site of the small nuclear RNA to form the core snRNP (Sm core). To assemble core snRNPs, the SMN complex accepts the trapped 5Sm proteins from CLNS1A forming an intermediate. Within the SMN complex, SMN1 acts as a structural backbone and together with GEMIN2 it gathers the Sm complex subunits. Binding of snRNA inside 5Sm ultimately triggers eviction of the SMN complex, thereby allowing binding of SNRPD3 and SNRPB to complete assembly of the core snRNP. Ensures the correct splicing of U12 intron- containing genes that may be important for normal motor and proprioceptive neurons development. Also required for resolving RNA-DNA hybrids created by RNA polymerase II, that form R- loop in transcription terminal regions, an important step in proper transcription termination. gene.name: superoxide dismutase 1
gene.function: Destroys radicals which are normally produced within the cells and which are toxic to biological systems. Catalyzes the oxidation of hydrogen sulfide (H2S) to sulfate, playing an important role in detoxifying H2S and limiting the accumulation of reactive sulfur species (RSS) such as persulfides and polysulfides.

phenotype.definition: Any cardiac rhythm other than the normal sinus rhythm. Such a rhythm may be either of sinus or ectopic origin and either regular or irregular. An arrhythmia may be due to a disturbance in impulse formation or conduction or both.

Increased size of the heart, clinically defined as an increased transverse diameter of the cardiac silhouette that is greater than or equal to 50% of the transverse diameter of the chest (increased cardiothoracic ratio) on a posterior-anterior projection of a chest radiograph or a computed tomography.

A myocardial disorder in which the heart muscle is structurally and functionally abnormal, in the absence of coronary artery disease, hypertension, valvular disease and congenital heart disease sufficient to cause the observed myocardial abnormality.
Onset of disease at the age of between 1 and 5 years.
A decrease in the strength of the diaphragm.
An abnormal increase in the size of the kidney.
A subjective feeling of tiredness characterized by a lack of energy and motivation.
Abnormally increased size of the liver.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is defined by the presence of increased ventricular wall thickness or mass in the absence of loading conditions (hypertension, valve disease) sufficient to cause the observed abnormality.

Hypotonia is an abnormally low muscle tone (the amount of tension or resistance to movement in a muscle). Even when relaxed, muscles have a continuous and passive partial contraction which provides some resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia thus manifests as diminished resistance to passive stretching. Hypotonia is not the same as muscle weakness, although the two conditions can co-exist.
Weakness of the limb-girdle muscles (also known as the pelvic and shoulder girdles), that is, lack of strength of the muscles around the shoulders and the pelvis.
Inability to walk in a person who previous had the ability to walk.
Reduced strength of muscles.
Lack of strength of the proximal muscles that becomes progressively more severe.
A lack of strength of the proximal muscles.
The upper eyelid margin is positioned 3 mm or more lower than usual and covers the superior portion of the iris (objective); or, the upper lid margin obscures at least part of the pupil (subjective).

Respiratory distress is objectively observable as the physical or emotional consequences from the experience of dyspnea. The physical presentation of respiratory distress is generally referred to as labored breathing, while the sensation of respiratory distress is called shortness of breath or dyspnea.
A severe form of respiratory insufficiency characterized by inadequate gas exchange such that the levels of oxygen or carbon dioxide cannot be maintained within normal limits.

evidence.quote: Pompe disease, also referred to as glycogen storage disorder type II or acid maltase deficiency, is a lysosomal storage disorder (LSD) caused by mutations in the GAA gene
Lysosomal glycogen accumulation in Pompe disease is due to deficiency of the enzyme acid α-glucosidase (GAA), which breaks down glycogen in the lysosomes.

Pompe disease (OMIM 23200), also referred to as glycogen storage disease type II or acid maltase deficiency, is a lysosomal storage disease (LSD) caused by mutations in the gene (GAA) that encodes the lysosomal hydrolase acid α-glucosidase (GAA)
Pompe disease (PD; OMIM 232300) is a severe metabolic myopathy caused by the deficiency of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA; acid maltase, E.C.3.2.1.20)

Pompe disease (also known as glycogen storage disease type 2 or acid maltase deficiency) is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by mutations in the gene that encodes the hydrolase acid α-glucosidase (GAA)
PD is a metabolic disorder, with an estimated incidence of 1:40,000 live births, caused by defective activity of the lysosomal hydrolase acid α-glucosidase (GAA, acid maltase).
Pompe disease is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder, whereby mutations in the GAA gene lead to partial or total absence of the lysosomal enzyme acid α-glucosidase.
Pompe disease, a relentlessly progressive, autosomal recessive myopathy caused by a deficiency of acid α-glucosidase.

Pompe disease (OMIM 232300; acid maltase deficiency, glycogen storage disease type II) is an autosomal recessive deficiency of lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA; OMIM 606800) that results in progressive glycogen accumulation
PD is caused by mutations in the acid α-glucosidase (GAA) gene, encoding the lysosomal hydrolase α-glucosidase (acid maltase, GAA, E.C.3.2.1.20).

papers.title: Duvoglustat HCl Increases Systemic and Tissue Exposure of Active Acid α-Glucosidase in Pompe Patients Co-administered with Alglucosidase α.
papers.summary: In a phase 2a single-dose study of 25 adults with Pompe disease, oral duvoglustat HCl co-administered with alglucosidase alfa increased systemic exposure and skeletal-muscle levels of active acid α-glucosidase compared with alglucosidase alfa alone. The co-administration was generally well tolerated, but the single-dose study did not establish clinical benefit, clear dose-response relationships for muscle activity, or significant between-dose differences.
papers.why: A phase 2a study in Pompe patients shows that oral duvoglustat increases exposure and activity of infused alglucosidase alfa in plasma and skeletal muscle.

papers.title: Efficacy and Safety of Avalglucosidase Alfa in Patients With Late-Onset Pompe Disease After 97 Weeks: A Phase 3 Randomized Clinical Trial.
papers.summary: In the COMET extension, avalglucosidase alfa maintained or improved respiratory function, functional endurance, motor function, muscle strength, and health-related quality of life through 97 weeks in patients with late-onset Pompe disease. Patients switching from alglucosidase alfa generally stabilized after switching, although improvements were smaller than in patients initially treated with avalglucosidase alfa, and no new safety or immunogenicity concerns were observed.
papers.why: A phase 3 randomized extension trial provides patient efficacy and safety data for avalglucosidase alfa in late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: Cipaglucosidase Alfa: First Approval.
papers.summary: Cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat is a two-component enzyme replacement approach for Pompe disease: recombinant human GAA cleaves lysosomal glycogen, while miglustat stabilizes the enzyme during infusion. Clinical studies showed reductions in muscle-damage and glycogen-accumulation biomarkers and potential motor or respiratory benefits, but the phase III PROPEL trial did not demonstrate superiority over alglucosidase alfa for the primary 6-minute walk distance endpoint.
papers.why: The article reports the development and regulatory approval of cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat as an existing treatment for late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: 104-week efficacy and safety of cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat in adults with late-onset Pompe disease: a phase III open-label extension study (ATB200-07).
papers.summary: In this open-label phase III extension, cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat maintained motor-function, muscle-strength and biomarker improvements or stabilized respiratory and patient-reported outcomes for up to 104 weeks in adults with late-onset Pompe disease, including after switching from alglucosidase alfa. Treatment was generally well tolerated, but infusion-associated reactions occurred, and the uncontrolled descriptive design, small ERT-naïve subgroup and short follow-up limit certainty about comparative long-term efficacy.
papers.why: A phase 3 open-label extension provides long-term efficacy, biomarker, and safety data for cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat in adults with late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: The pharmacological chaperone AT2220 increases recombinant human acid α-glucosidase uptake and glycogen reduction in a mouse model of Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The paper shows that the pharmacological chaperone AT2220 stabilizes recombinant human acid α-glucosidase (rhGAA), prolongs its circulation, and increases its uptake and activity in heart and skeletal muscles of GAA knock-out mice. Co-administration with rhGAA produced greater glycogen reduction than rhGAA alone, but did not normalize tissue glycogen or GAA activity to wild-type levels and was evaluated only in preclinical models.
papers.why: Preclinical and in vitro data show that AT2220 stabilizes recombinant GAA and increases its circulation, tissue uptake, and glycogen reduction in a Pompe disease mouse model.

papers.title: A study on the safety and efficacy of reveglucosidase alfa in patients with late-onset Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a first-in-human phase 1/2 open-label study, reveglucosidase alfa was generally tolerated in 22 previously enzyme-replacement-naive patients with late-onset Pompe disease and was associated with improved respiratory muscle strength, maximum voluntary ventilation, and walking distance through 72 weeks. Stable forced vital capacity, limited walking benefit, and frequent hypoglycemia and hypersensitivity reactions temper the findings, and the absence of pre-planned statistical analyses limits efficacy conclusions.
papers.why: A clinical study directly tested the pharmacokinetics, safety, and exploratory efficacy of the IGF2-tagged enzyme reveglucosidase alfa in late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: Enhanced efficacy of enzyme replacement therapy in Pompe disease through mannose-6-phosphate receptor expression in skeletal muscle.
papers.summary: In mouse models of Pompe disease, skeletal-muscle deletion of the cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor impaired recombinant human GAA uptake, reduced biochemical correction, and prevented glycogen clearance after enzyme replacement therapy. Conversely, clenbuterol increased CI-MPR expression and enhanced the biochemical and early functional efficacy of GAA replacement therapy, although increased perfusion and glycogenolysis could not be excluded as additional mechanisms.
papers.why: Pompe disease mouse experiments show that clenbuterol increases skeletal-muscle CI-MPR expression and enhances biochemical and glycogen-reducing efficacy of enzyme replacement therapy.

papers.title: Transcription factor EB (TFEB) is a new therapeutic target for Pompe disease.
papers.summary: TFEB overexpression cleared lysosomal glycogen, reduced enlarged lysosomes, and alleviated autophagic accumulation in Pompe disease myotubes, isolated muscle fibres, and GAA-knockout mice. The effects depended strongly on intact autophagy, whereas pharmacological mTORC1 inhibition with Torin 1 or Torin 2 failed to reproduce lysosomal clearance; constitutively active TFEB also caused myotube morphological changes and occasional apoptosis.
papers.why: TFEB overexpression reduced glycogen accumulation, lysosomal enlargement, and autophagic-vacuole accumulation in cell and mouse models of Pompe disease.

papers.title: Structure of human lysosomal acid α-glucosidase-a guide for the treatment of Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The paper presents high-resolution crystal structures of recombinant human lysosomal acid α-glucosidase (rhGAA) alone and bound to inhibitors or the allosteric pharmacological chaperone N-acetylcysteine. The structures define GAA substrate-binding features, active-site and allosteric ligand interactions, and provide a structural framework for mapping Pompe disease mutations and developing pharmacological chaperones; the paper does not report a new clinical treatment trial.
papers.why: The structural models explain GAA substrate and inhibitor recognition and reveal the molecular basis for N-acetylcysteine-mediated GAA stabilization.

papers.title: The pharmacological chaperone N-butyldeoxynojirimycin enhances enzyme replacement therapy in Pompe disease fibroblasts.
papers.summary: The study shows that combining the pharmacological chaperone N-butyldeoxynojirimycin with recombinant human acid α-glucosidase enhances enzyme replacement in Pompe disease fibroblasts and a knockout mouse model by increasing lysosomal delivery, maturation, and stability of the recombinant enzyme. A parallel experiment in Fabry disease fibroblasts indicates that this enhancement is enzyme-specific: 1-deoxygalactonojirimycin enhanced recombinant α-galactosidase A correction, whereas N-butyldeoxynojirimycin had no effect.
papers.why: NB-DNJ enhanced recombinant GAA delivery, maturation, stability, and enzyme correction in Pompe fibroblasts and Gaa-knockout mice.

papers.title: Clinical features and predictors for disease natural progression in adults with Pompe disease: a nationwide prospective observational study.
papers.summary: In a prospective observational cohort of 94 untreated adults with Pompe disease, muscle strength and pulmonary function deteriorated over an average 1.6 years, while disease duration of at least 15 years and baseline forced vital capacity below 80% predicted faster muscle-strength decline. The study also identifies clinical patterns, diagnostic measures, and quantitative outcome measures useful for recognizing and monitoring adult Pompe disease.
papers.why: This prospective study establishes longitudinal muscle and pulmonary outcome measures and identifies prognostic factors for adult Pompe disease progression.

papers.title: Large variation in effects during 10 years of enzyme therapy in adults with Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a 10-year prospective cohort of 30 adults with late-onset Pompe disease, enzyme replacement therapy with alglucosidase alfa initially benefited 93% of patients, but many experienced secondary deterioration after approximately 3–5 years. Group-level walking ability, muscle strength, and pulmonary function declined by year 10, although pulmonary function remained better than the extrapolated untreated course, and individual responses varied substantially.
papers.why: Ten-year prospective evidence quantifies long-term ERT benefits and variability using longitudinal walking, strength, and pulmonary-function endpoints.

papers.title: Algorithm for the early diagnosis and treatment of patients with cross reactive immunologic material-negative classic infantile pompe disease: a step towards improving the efficacy of ERT.
papers.summary: This paper reports an observational clinical study of seven CRIM-negative patients with classic infantile Pompe disease who received early enzyme replacement therapy with alglucosidase alfa plus an immune tolerance induction regimen of rituximab, methotrexate, and IVIG. Compared with historical CRIM-negative patients treated with ERT monotherapy, the combined regimen was associated with lower anti-rhGAA antibody titers, improved cardiomyopathy, prolonged invasive-ventilator-free survival, and no major protocol-attributed infections or major laboratory toxicity, although residual weakness and feeding difficulties remained.
papers.why: The clinical algorithm rapidly identifies CRIM-negative infantile Pompe patients and combines ERT with immunomodulation to reduce anti-drug antibodies and improve outcomes.

papers.title: Abnormal mannose-6-phosphate receptor trafficking impairs recombinant alpha-glucosidase uptake in Pompe disease fibroblasts.
papers.summary: In Pompe disease patient fibroblasts, abnormal lysosomal glycogen storage, autophagic-compartment expansion, Golgi disorganization, and disrupted cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor trafficking correlate with disease severity and impair uptake and lysosomal processing of recombinant human GAA. Continuous recombinant human GAA treatment gradually restores GAA activity and partially rescues CI-MPR localization, with severe-disease fibroblasts requiring longer exposure; defective recombinant GAA uptake was also observed in fibroblasts from other lysosomal storage disease models.
papers.why: Provides Pompe patient fibroblast data identifying CI-MPR trafficking as a determinant of recombinant GAA uptake and a mechanism for optimizing enzyme replacement therapy.

papers.title: GAA variants and phenotypes among 1,079 patients with Pompe disease: Data from the Pompe Registry.
papers.summary: The Pompe Registry analysis identified 2,075 GAA variants in 1,079 patients, including 80 unique novel variants, and provided preliminary pathogenicity classifications and phenotype correlations. The study also highlights diagnostic gaps, pseudodeficiency alleles, computational prediction limitations, and the need for functional and complete genotype–phenotype studies.
papers.why: The Pompe Registry provides a large disease-specific resource and variant classification framework supporting GAA diagnosis, prognosis, and outcome prediction.

papers.title: Long term clinical history of an Italian cohort of infantile onset Pompe disease treated with enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 28 Italian infants with infantile onset Pompe disease, alglucosidase alfa enzyme replacement therapy was associated with cardiac normalization and survival but did not prevent progressive motor, respiratory, or central nervous system deterioration over a median follow-up of 71 months. CRIM-positive patients generally had better outcomes than CRIM-negative patients, although several CRIM-positive patients continued to deteriorate and some required immunomodulation or desensitization for anti-rhGAA antibody-related reactions.
papers.why: This long-term infantile Pompe cohort links early alglucosidase alfa treatment and CRIM status to survival, ventilation, ambulation, motor, cardiac, and respiratory outcomes.

papers.title: CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease: characterization of immune responses in patients treated with ERT monotherapy.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 20 CRIM-negative infants with Pompe disease receiving alglucosidase alfa monotherapy, 85% developed clinically significant anti-rhGAA IgG antibodies, with high sustained titers associated with invasive ventilation or death. The findings associate nonsense GAA variants with high antibody titers, show that early enzyme replacement therapy alone does not prevent immune responses, and support immune tolerance induction in the treatment-naïve setting.
papers.why: Patient data identify anti-rhGAA antibodies and CRIM status as major ERT-response biomarkers and support immune-tolerance strategies to prevent treatment failure.

papers.title: Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease.
papers.summary: This review describes newborn screening and molecular diagnosis for Pompe disease, emphasizing AαGlu activity measurement in dried blood spots followed by GAA gene analysis, while documenting false-positive results and interference from GAA pseudodeficiency alleles. It also summarizes evidence that early enzyme replacement therapy improves outcomes in infantile-onset Pompe disease, while highlighting the risk of neutralizing antibodies, the need for CRIM evaluation, and uncertainty surrounding treatment of presymptomatic late-onset disease.
papers.why: Describes validated newborn-screening assays and the combination of enzyme and GAA genetic testing needed to distinguish Pompe disease from pseudodeficiency.

papers.title: Extension of the Pompe mutation database by linking disease-associated variants to clinical severity.
papers.summary: The study extended the Pompe disease GAA variant database by linking 562 GAA variants, including information from 867 patients, to clinical severity, CRIM status, splicing predictions, minor allele frequency, and biochemical evidence. It identifies genotype–phenotype relationships useful for diagnosis, prognosis, treatment selection, and experimental prioritization, while emphasizing that computational predictions require experimental confirmation and that the database has incomplete geographic coverage.
papers.why: Extends a Pompe-specific variant database with clinical severity, CRIM status, and functional predictions supported by analysis of 562 GAA variants and 867 patients.

papers.title: The clinical relevance of outcomes used in late-onset Pompe disease: can we do better?
papers.summary: This review finds that 6-minute walk test and forced vital capacity changes during alglucosidase alfa treatment often reached minimal clinically important difference thresholds extrapolated from chronic respiratory diseases in late-onset Pompe disease, but the clinical relevance of these thresholds in Pompe disease remains unestablished. It recommends disease-specific validation and highlights SNIP, MIP, MEP, GSCG, R-PAct, and composite neuromuscular measures as potentially more clinically relevant alternatives or adjuncts.
papers.why: The study critically analyzes clinical relevance and minimal important differences for Pompe disease endpoints and identifies more disease-appropriate neuromuscular outcome measures.

papers.title: Transforming the clinical outcome in CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease identified via newborn screening: the benefits of early treatment with enzyme replacement therapy and immune tolerance induction.
papers.summary: In a retrospective international cohort of 20 infants with CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease, initiation of enzyme replacement therapy plus prophylactic immune tolerance induction within the first four weeks of life was associated with better survival, cardiac, respiratory, feeding, motor, and biomarker outcomes than later treatment. The very small early-treatment group and nonrandomized comparison with a historical enzyme-replacement-therapy monotherapy cohort limit causal and long-term conclusions.
papers.why: Reports improved cardiac, motor, pulmonary, and biomarker outcomes when early ERT is combined with prophylactic immune tolerance induction in CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease.

papers.title: Childhood Pompe disease: clinical spectrum and genotype in 31 patients.
papers.summary: This cross-sectional observational study of 31 untreated children with non-classic Pompe disease found substantial clinical heterogeneity, including early limb-girdle and neck-flexor weakness, reduced muscle strength, restrictive pulmonary impairment, and occasional hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. Diagnosis was established by acid α-glucosidase activity measurement and GAA mutation analysis, while elevated CK, AST, and ALT were common potential diagnostic clues.
papers.why: The untreated pediatric cohort provides longitudinal natural-history data and clinically useful measures of mobility, respiratory, and cardiac progression in Pompe disease.

papers.title: Genotype-phenotype correlation in Pompe disease, a step forward.
papers.summary: In 85 late-onset Pompe disease patients carrying the GAA c.-32-13T > G allele, the c.-32-13T > G/c.1927G > A genotype was associated with shorter disease-free survival. The ACE DD and ACTN3 XX genotypes were associated with earlier disease onset, while ACE DD was also associated with muscle pain; AGT, PPARα, and most tested clinical severity measures showed no significant modifier associations.
papers.why: The study identifies ACE and ACTN3 polymorphisms as modifiers of Pompe disease onset and muscle pain while validating several clinical severity and progression measures.

papers.title: The First Year Experience of Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease in California.
papers.summary: California's first year of universal newborn screening identified 18Pompe disease cases among 453,152 newborns using a two-tier process of flow injection analysis-tandem mass spectrometry for GAA enzyme activity followed by GAA gene sequencing. Lower GAA activity distinguished classic infantile-onset disease from suspected late-onset disease, while pseudodeficiency alleles, variants of uncertain significance, and overlap between disease and nondisease activity values complicated interpretation.
papers.why: The report validates a population-scale GAA activity plus sequencing screening workflow and provides newborn prevalence and variant-frequency data.

papers.title: Targeted approaches to induce immune tolerance for Pompe disease therapy.
papers.summary: This review identifies immune responses to GAA and viral vector components as major barriers to effective Pompe disease treatment, while highlighting ERT, gene therapy, GILT-GAA, chaperones, and immune-modulation strategies that improve treatment efficacy or induce tolerance. Preclinical and limited clinical evidence supports liver-directed, hematopoietic stem-cell, oral, red-blood-cell, and vector-based approaches, but several strategies remain experimental and have not yet established a universally accepted clinical standard.
papers.why: This review reports tested strategies for overcoming anti-GAA and anti-vector immune responses that limit enzyme and gene replacement therapy in Pompe disease.

papers.title: Long-term Safety and Efficacy of Avalglucosidase Alfa in Patients With Late-Onset Pompe Disease.
papers.summary: The NEO1/NEO-EXT open-label extension study provides Class IV evidence that avalglucosidase alfa was generally well tolerated for up to 6.5 years in adults with late-onset Pompe disease. Respiratory and walking outcomes were generally stabilized, while urinary Hex4 and creatine kinase tended to decrease; the uncontrolled, small study and use of lower initial doses limit causal interpretation.
papers.why: This long-term study provides up to 6.5 years of safety and efficacy data for avalglucosidase alfa in late-onset Pompe disease, including pulmonary and walking outcomes.

papers.title: A genetic modifier of symptom onset in Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The study identifies GAA c.510C>T as a cis-acting genetic modifier of Pompe disease: in compound heterozygous or homozygous IVS1 patients, it worsens exon 2 splicing, lowers residual wild-type GAA expression and enzyme activity, and is associated with earlier or more frequent symptoms. The variant can be detected by allele-specific PCR and Sanger sequencing, improving prognostic interpretation and timing of enzyme replacement therapy in newborn screening and standard diagnostics.
papers.why: The study validates c.510C>T as a genetic modifier of IVS1-associated Pompe disease and shows that allele-specific genotyping and splicing analysis can improve prediction of symptom onset.

papers.title: Lung MRI and impairment of diaphragmatic function in Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a cross-sectional study of ten adults with Pompe disease, lung MRI showed severe impairment of diaphragmatic displacement, with some patients exhibiting almost no movement. Normalized cranial-caudal lung-length change was strongly correlated with supine forced vital capacity and postural drop, suggesting that MRI and these spirometry measures can provide information about diaphragmatic dysfunction, while the response of pulmonary function to enzyme replacement therapy was described in prior work as limited.
papers.why: The study validates lung MRI as a method for quantifying severely impaired diaphragmatic and chest-wall motion in Pompe disease.

papers.title: Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease: Pennsylvania Experience.
papers.summary: Pennsylvania newborn screening using dried-blood-spot GAA enzyme activity followed by full GAA gene sequencing identified infantile-onset, late-onset, and suspected late-onset Pompe disease while also identifying carriers, pseudodeficiency carriers, and false-positive results. GAA activity and creatine kinase helped distinguish groups at the cohort level, but overlapping values limited individual classification, while Hex4 was useful in infantile-onset disease but normal in all diagnosed late-onset cases in this cohort.
papers.why: Provides large-scale validation of a two-tier newborn-screening workflow using flow-injection tandem mass spectrometry followed by GAA sequencing.

papers.title: Metabolomic Profiling of Pompe Disease-Induced Pluripotent Stem Cell-Derived Cardiomyocytes Reveals That Oxidative Stress Is Associated with Cardiac and Skeletal Muscle Pathology.
papers.summary: The study shows that late-onset Pompe disease iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and a Gaa-deficient mouse model exhibit oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and reduced NRF-2/ARE-mediated antioxidant signaling. Oltipraz, an NRF-2 activator, reduced GSSG production and reactive oxygen species levels in Pompe disease iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, identifying oxidative stress as a candidate therapeutic target.
papers.why: The study develops and characterizes a Pompe iPSC-cardiomyocyte model, applies metabolomic profiling, and validates disease-associated oxidative-stress changes in human and murine cells.

papers.title: Gene Therapy Developments for Pompe Disease.
papers.summary: This review identifies GAA deficiency as the cause of lysosomal glycogen accumulation and multisystem Pompe disease pathology, while emphasizing limitations of enzyme replacement therapy, including incomplete tissue delivery, CNS exclusion, immunogenicity, and lifelong treatment. It describes promising preclinical and clinical-development strategies based on AAV and lentiviral HSPC gene therapy, alongside protein engineering, antisense oligonucleotides, genome editing, and new disease models, with important delivery, biodistribution, immunogenicity, and safety limitations.
papers.why: The review describes gene-therapy platforms developed and tested for Pompe disease, including strategies to improve tissue expression, secretion, uptake, and systemic or CNS delivery.

papers.title: Update of the Pompe variant database for the prediction of clinical phenotypes: Novel disease-associated variants, common sequence variants, and results from newborn screening.
papers.summary: The paper updates a curated Pompe disease GAA variant database with 226 newly identified disease-associated variants, 148 common nondisease-associated variants, and findings from newborn screening. Functional testing showed that seven selected missense variants abrogate GAA activity in transfected COS-7 cells, supporting severity predictions and molecular diagnosis while highlighting uncertainty for variants found only in newborn screening.
papers.why: Updates a curated disease-specific variant database with functional and computational evidence to improve variant interpretation and genotype-phenotype prediction.

papers.title: Disease modeling and lentiviral gene transfer in patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells from late-onset Pompe disease patient.
papers.summary: The study generated patient-specific iPSC lines and iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes from a patient with late-onset Pompe disease that reproduced lysosomal glycogen accumulation, reduced GAA activity, and lysosomal enlargement. Third-generation lentiviral GAA gene transfer increased enzyme activity, localized GAA to lysosomes, and ameliorated biochemical and ultrastructural abnormalities before and after cardiomyocyte differentiation, although glycogen content was not fully normalized within 48 hours.
papers.why: Pompe-specific iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes reproduced glycogen accumulation and lysosomal enlargement, and lentiviral GAA rescue improved enzyme activity and pathology.

papers.title: Three-dimensional tissue-engineered human skeletal muscle model of Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The study establishes a three-dimensional primary human skeletal-muscle myobundle model of infantile-onset Pompe disease that reproduces low GAA activity, glycogen accumulation, lysosomal enlargement, stress-sensitive functional deficits, and disease-associated transcriptional changes. Recombinant human GAA and AAV-mediated hGAA increase enzyme activity and clear glycogen but produce only partial molecular rescue and do not correct stress-induced contractile deficits in the tested seven-day in vitro conditions.
papers.why: A patient-derived three-dimensional muscle model reproduced Pompe pathology and was used to test enzyme replacement and AAV gene delivery, with transcriptomic profiling identifying disease pathways.

papers.title: Characterization of immune response in Cross-Reactive Immunological Material (CRIM)-positive infantile Pompe disease patients treated with enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.summary: In a retrospective analysis of 37 CRIM-positive infants with Pompe disease receiving alglucosidase alfa without immune modulation, 12 developed anti-rhGAA IgG titers of at least 12,800 and had significantly greater left ventricular mass index than the low-titer group at week 78. GAA variant patterns showed statistical trends, but variants alone could not predict the antibody response; HLA-based individualized T-cell epitope measurement is proposed as a possible risk-assessment approach requiring future validation.
papers.why: In 37 CRIM-positive infantile Pompe patients receiving ERT, longitudinal antibody titers identified HSAT/SIT groups that may compromise treatment response.

papers.title: Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease in Illinois: Experience with 684,290 Infants.
papers.summary: Illinois statewide newborn screening identified 29 definitive cases of Pompe disease among 684,290 infants, including three infantile-onset and 26 late-onset cases, while producing false-positive results from pseudodeficiency and carrier status. The screened infants treated with alglucosidase alfa had favorable reported clinical outcomes, although follow-up data were incomplete and long-term treatment decisions for late-onset disease remained uncertain.
papers.why: A statewide program screened 684,290 infants and identified 29 Pompe cases while detecting carriers, pseudodeficiency, and inconclusive results requiring follow-up.

papers.title: Benefits of Prophylactic Short-Course Immune Tolerance Induction in Patients With Infantile Pompe Disease: Demonstration of Long-Term Safety and Efficacy in an Expanded Cohort.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 34 infants with infantile Pompe disease, short-course prophylactic immune tolerance induction with rituximab, methotrexate, and intravenous immunoglobulin alongside enzyme replacement therapy maintained low or absent anti-rhGAA antibody titers in 88% of patients and was associated with improved cardiac and respiratory outcomes. Transient neutropenia, liver-enzyme elevation, and infections occurred, but all 33 evaluable patients achieved B-cell reconstitution and no deaths were attributed to immunomodulation.
papers.why: The expanded cohort supports short-course rituximab-based immune tolerance induction before ERT as a safe approach associated with sustained low anti-GAA antibody titers.

papers.title: An immune tolerance approach using transient low-dose methotrexate in the ERT-naïve setting of patients treated with a therapeutic protein: experience in infantile-onset Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a small, nonrandomized cohort of 14 treatment-naïve patients with infantile-onset Pompe disease, three cycles of transient low-dose methotrexate initiated with recombinant human acid α-glucosidase were associated with fewer sustained intermediate or high anti-rhGAA IgG antibody titers than in a historical ERT-monotherapy cohort. The regimen was generally tolerable, but transient neutropenia, elevated liver enzymes, and infection-related hospitalizations occurred, and efficacy requires larger controlled studies.
papers.why: Co-initiation of transient low-dose methotrexate with rhGAA was associated with sustained low antibody titers in 12 of 14 CRIM-positive infantile Pompe patients.

papers.title: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) in Belgium: clinical characteristics and outcome measures.
papers.summary: In a Belgian cohort of 52 patients with late-onset Pompe disease, longitudinal follow-up showed significant deterioration measured by 6MWD, MRC sum score, and sitting and supine FVC despite enzyme replacement therapy. The study also documented variable clinical presentation, a long diagnostic delay, prevalent and novel GAA variants, intracranial vascular abnormalities, and outcome-measure sensitivity, with 6MWD being more sensitive than ActivLim for longitudinal follow-up.
papers.why: Longitudinal data identify 6-minute walk distance, MRC sum score, and sitting or supine FVC as useful clinical endpoints and show that ActivLim and 10MWT were less sensitive in late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: Lessons Learned from Pompe Disease Newborn Screening and Follow-up.
papers.summary: Missouri universal newborn screening identified 46 cases of Pompe disease among approximately 467,000 newborns and showed that age- and season-adjusted GAA activity cutoffs plus multi-enzyme quality assessment can reduce false-positive referrals. Early enzyme replacement therapy was associated with stable or improved development and cardiac findings in most followed infants with Pompe disease, although infusion reactions and progressive myopathy occurred in isolated cases.
papers.why: Reports real-world implementation and six years of outcomes from a population-based Pompe newborn-screening and follow-up program.

papers.title: The pharmacological chaperone AT2220 increases the specific activity and lysosomal delivery of mutant acid alpha-glucosidase, and promotes glycogen reduction in a transgenic mouse model of Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The study shows that AT2220 (duvoglustat hydrochloride) acts as a pharmacological chaperone for several responsive mutant GAA proteins, increasing their catalytic activity, ER export, lysosomal delivery and stability. In the hP545L GAA Tg/KO mouse model of Pompe disease, oral AT2220 increased tissue GAA activity and reduced glycogen accumulation, with less-frequent regimens producing greater glycogen reduction than daily dosing.
papers.why: Oral AT2220 stabilized and lysosomally delivered mutant GAA in a transgenic Pompe mouse model while increasing tissue GAA activity and reducing glycogen accumulation.

papers.title: Newborn screening for Pompe disease in Italy: Long-term results and future challenges.
papers.summary: A seven-year Italian newborn-screening study identified 39 GAA-deficient neonates, including three infantile-onset and eight late-onset Pompe disease cases. Urinary Glc4 combined with left ventricular mass index rapidly distinguished infantile-onset disease, while prompt alglucosidase alfa treatment produced favorable outcomes in infantile-onset patients; enzyme-activity assays did not fully distinguish disease from pseudodeficiency or carrier status.
papers.why: Long-term newborn-screening data validate early diagnosis and ERT outcomes and identify urinary glucose tetrasaccharide as a useful severity and treatment-response biomarker.

papers.title: An analysis of Pompe newborn screening data: a new prevalence at birth, insight and discussion.
papers.summary: Analysis of 11,619,662 newborns screened across 22 states and 8 countries estimated the birth prevalence of Pompe disease at 1:18,711, with little evidence of ancestry-related differences in total prevalence. The paper also supports direct newborn screening using low GAA enzyme activity plus pathogenic GAA variants and proposes binomial analysis and power calculations to assess prevalence-estimate reliability.
papers.why: The study aggregates results from 11.6 million newborns and provides a substantial Pompe screening dataset plus methods for estimating birth prevalence.

papers.title: Pompe disease in Austria: clinical, genetic and epidemiological aspects.
papers.summary: This Austrian retrospective observational cohort identified 25 patients with infantile-onset or late-onset Pompe disease and characterized their genotypes, phenotypes, diagnostic delays, and responses to enzyme replacement therapy. The study found that enzyme replacement therapy improved cardiomyopathy in children with classical infantile-onset disease, but standardized follow-up in the small late-onset cohort suggested preserved mean forced vital capacity and a trend toward declining 6-minute walk distance.
papers.why: The survey supplies a national Pompe cohort and standardized longitudinal pulmonary and walking outcomes while documenting treatment use in affected patients.

papers.title: A nonsense mutation in the acid α-glucosidase gene causes Pompe disease in Finnish and Swedish Lapphunds.
papers.summary: The paper identifies the homozygous GAA c.2237G>A (p.W746*) nonsense mutation as the cause of Pompe disease in Finnish and Swedish Lapphunds and shows that affected dogs genetically and clinically resemble humans with classic infantile Pompe disease. The Finnish and Swedish Lapphunds are therefore proposed as large-animal models for preclinical gene-therapy development, while the mutation enables a genetic test for these Scandinavian breeds.
papers.why: The paper establishes genetically and clinicopathologically relevant canine Pompe models useful for preclinical gene-therapy studies.

papers.title: From Cryptic Toward Canonical Pre-mRNA Splicing in Pompe Disease: a Pipeline for the Development of Antisense Oligonucleotides.
papers.summary: The study identifies GAA variants that create or activate cryptic splice sites in Pompe disease and uses variant-directed phosphorodiamidate morpholino antisense oligonucleotides to redirect pre-mRNA splicing toward canonical splicing. In patient-derived fibroblasts, these oligonucleotides reduced aberrant GAA transcripts and increased GAA enzymatic activity, but efficacy in muscle cells, animals, patients, and correction of glycogen storage remain untested.
papers.why: The study directly develops a transferable screening and ASO correction pipeline and shows splice-site repression with increased GAA activity in Pompe patient variants.

papers.title: Long-term follow-up of 17 patients with childhood Pompe disease treated with enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.summary: In a prospective 17-year cohort of children with non-classic Pompe disease, enzyme replacement therapy was generally associated with preserved or improved motor function and muscle strength over seven years, while lung function declined overall. Responses varied markedly between patients, and one patient with severe baseline impairment showed a clear cardiac response but little apparent motor or respiratory benefit.
papers.why: The prospective seven-year study provides long-term evidence for ERT efficacy in childhood Pompe disease using validated muscle-function and lung-function endpoints.

papers.title: Light and Shadows in Newborn Screening for Lysosomal Storage Disorders: Eight Years of Experience in Northeast Italy.
papers.summary: In a regional newborn-screening cohort, low dried-blood-spot GAA activity identified infants with infantile- or late-onset Pompe disease, while urinary Glc4, cardiologic assessment, and molecular analysis supported confirmation and subtype assignment. Early alglucosidase alfa treatment produced favorable outcomes in two CRIM-positive infants, whereas one CRIM-negative infant developed anti-rhGAA antibodies with persistent cardiomyopathy and psychomotor delay.
papers.why: Large-scale implementation data demonstrate the feasibility of tandem-mass-spectrometry newborn screening with biomarker confirmation, including for Pompe disease.

papers.title: The Latin American experience with a next generation sequencing genetic panel for recessive limb-girdle muscular weakness and Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In 2,103 Latin American patients with undiagnosed proximal muscle weakness, a targeted 10-gene next-generation sequencing panel identified nine patients with Pompe disease, and low measured GAA activity corroborated the diagnosis in tested siblings. Including GAA and targeted deep intronic variants improved Pompe disease detection, while the study reported substantial variant-of-unknown-significance and technical limitations.
papers.why: A targeted NGS panel evaluated 2,103 proximal-weakness patients and identified Pompe disease cases, demonstrating a reusable diagnostic workflow.

papers.title: The European reference network for metabolic diseases (MetabERN) clinical pathway recommendations for Pompe disease (acid maltase deficiency, glycogen storage disease type II).
papers.summary: This review describes Pompe disease as an autosomal recessive lysosomal metabolic myopathy caused by biallelic pathogenic GAA variants and lysosomal glycogen accumulation. It identifies diagnostic standards, outcome measures, supportive resources, and recombinant human GAA therapies, reporting clinical improvement or stabilization with alglucosidase alfa, avalglucosidase alfa, and cipaglucosidase alfa while noting monitoring, immune, and evidence limitations.
papers.why: This paper develops an evidence-graded clinical pathway and practical care standard covering diagnosis, therapy, monitoring, and follow-up in Pompe disease.
